The ZONOS3-Mini text-to-speech model is a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) with 800M total and 100M active parameters. It supports zero-shot voice cloning and word-level delivery control. Weights ship under Apache 2.0. For AI devs, size is the key point. It runs in a browser tab, on a laptop or on a server GPU. TL;DR Size: 800M total parameters, about 100M active per token (64 experts, top-2 routing); 32,768-position context; up to 10 minutes of audio per generation. Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via SGLang-Omni, Apple Silicon via MLX, CPU/CUDA/Metal/Vulkan via ggml, and phones or laptops via WebGPU in the browser. Performance: Ranks first among open models on Zyphra’s ZTTS2-Eval Capability Index (self-reported). Best: 80 ms median time to first audio on one H100 at 8 concurrent requests, and 457 seconds of audio per second peak throughput. Worst: Under 570 ms time to first audio in the browser on a Pixel 9, versus under 150 ms on an M3 MacBook Air. Bottom line: Best: frontier-level open TTS quality at 100M active parameters. Worst: every benchmark is run by Zyphra itself, and reference-clip cloning scores far lower than embedding mode. What is ZONOS3-Mini? ZONOS3-Mini is a compact zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model from Zyphra that runs in real time on-device. Zyphra trained it on 112 NVIDIA H100s in 2.5 days. It follows ZONOS2 , which used 8B parameters and an 86 Hz codec. That size limited where ZONOS2 could be deployed. How does the ZONOS3-Mini architecture work? Zyphra changed 3 layers of the stack : A new codec : Zyphra trained Zyphra Audio Codec 1 (ZAC-1) to replace the Descript Audio Codec. ZAC-1 runs at 15 Hz with 10 codebooks of 4,096 entries: 1 semantic and 9 acoustic. Zyphra reports a 10x word error rate reduction versus a DAC-trained model under similar data constraints. A causal iSTFT head renders each frame to 44.1 kHz audio as soon as it is generated. A hybrid MoE backbone : The model card lists 11 layers with model dimension 1,024. Sequence mixing follows a 3:1 ratio: 9 Gated DeltaNet layers and 2 global attention layers. Zyphra also adds latent MoE, Q balancing and attention residuals. A new speaker encoder : Voice representation moves from the Qwen3-TTS speaker encoder to MECT-B2. The model accepts a raw reference clip of up to 60 seconds, or a single 192-dimensional speaker embedding. Post-training used DPO, then GRPO, to improve robustness. How does word-level voice control work? Identity controls cover age, gender, accent and voice texture through speaker embedding vectors and accent task vectors. Delivery controls cover pace, emotion, projection and liveliness through activation steering. Learned alignment heads let steering apply to specific words during streaming. A separate edit model, based on a VoiceCraft recipe, can modify sentences after generation. The post Meta FAIR Releases e-means: An Algorithm Beating k-means in 10x Fewer Epochs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta FAIR researchers have released e-means , a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means algorithm. The e-means clustering algorithm reaches the loss Lloyd’s k-means gets in 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs . It ships in FAISS 1.16.0 under faiss.contrib.e_means . For anyone building vector indexes, quantizers or data-curation pipelines, clustering is often the slowest offline step. e-means targets exactly that step. TL;DR Size: It is an algorithm. Tested from 100K to 10 billion points, up to 16.7M clusters. Runs on: CPU or GPU, with PyTorch tensors or NumPy. Paper GPU runs use H100s. Performance: Lower loss than Lloyd’s k-means in roughly one-tenth the epochs, across 24 dataset configurations (self-reported). Best: 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedup over Flash-KMeans at equal loss. Worst: 16M-centroid runs need 64 GiB of float32 accumulators, so centroids must be sharded across GPUs. What is e-means? e-means is a mini-batch k-means algorithm from Meta FAIR that updates centroids with exponential moving averages. How does e-means work? Every k-means variant keeps a sum S and a count N per cluster. The centroid is S divided by N. Methods differ only in how S and N change. Lloyd recomputes S and N from the full dataset each iteration. MacQueen (1967) keeps adding batch statistics forever, so stale assignments never leave. e-means decays old statistics at rate α: S ← (1−α)S + αs, and the same for N. Older assignments fade, so centroids track recent data. The research team expa Lloyd is a corner case: full batch with α = 1. On DEEP, that corner sits 1.8% above the best loss. The team tested plain gradient descent as an alternative. At its best setting, it ended 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above EMA. The authors suspect EMA wins because centroids always stay inside the hull of their assigned points. What replaces hyperparameter tuning? Two fitted scaling laws set batch size B and initial step α0 from dataset size n, cluster count k and epochs T. On held-out datasets, median regret was 0.07% for the step law. The step then follows a cosine schedule from α0 to 0.1α0. What else changed? Dead-cluster revival: clusters below a size threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. Finalization: training ends on each cluster’s exact last-epoch mean. Fused GPU kernels: nearest-centroid assignment is fused, so saved epochs become saved seconds. [EMBED: e-means interactive explainer] How fast is e-means in benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported by the authors. Epochs: e-means beats Lloyd’s 25-epoch loss in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs. GPU: 10-45x wall-clock speedup against Flash-KMeans . CPU: 8-15x speedup against Faiss k-means. VIBE benchmark: all 11 embedding datasets needed 1.6 to 2.4 epochs. Billion scale: DINO10B, 10 billion 1,024-dim embeddings, split into 16.7M clusters in 2.5 epochs. The release thread shows a 1-CPU-thread demo. Lloyd took 4.39 s for 25 epochs. e-means took 0.43 s for 2.2 epochs. One Lloyd step touched 100,000 points (0.176 s). One e-means step touched 512 points (0.001 s). Mini-batch noise also helps escape bad local minima. On a 5-blob toy, Lloyd stayed stuck on 46% of 200 starts. e-means stayed stuck on 0%. Revival matters at large k. On DEEP with 16,384 clusters, proportional splitting left 47 dead clusters (0.3%). With revival off, 4,313 clusters (26.3%) died. How does e-means compare with other k-means options? The post Meta FAIR Releases e-means: An Algorithm Beating k-means in 10x Fewer Epochs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta FAIR researchers have released e-means , a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means algorithm. The e-means clustering algorithm reaches the loss Lloyd’s k-means gets in 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs . It ships in FAISS 1.16.0 under faiss.contrib.e_means . For anyone building vector indexes, quantizers or data-curation pipelines, clustering is often the slowest offline step. e-means targets exactly that step. TL;DR Size: It is an algorithm. Tested from 100K to 10 billion points, up to 16.7M clusters. Runs on: CPU or GPU, with PyTorch tensors or NumPy. Paper GPU runs use H100s. Performance: Lower loss than Lloyd’s k-means in roughly one-tenth the epochs, across 24 dataset configurations (self-reported). Best: 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedup over Flash-KMeans at equal loss. Worst: 16M-centroid runs need 64 GiB of float32 accumulators, so centroids must be sharded across GPUs. What is e-means? e-means is a mini-batch k-means algorithm from Meta FAIR that updates centroids with exponential moving averages. How does e-means work? Every k-means variant keeps a sum S and a count N per cluster. The centroid is S divided by N. Methods differ only in how S and N change. Lloyd recomputes S and N from the full dataset each iteration. MacQueen (1967) keeps adding batch statistics forever, so stale assignments never leave. e-means decays old statistics at rate α: S ← (1−α)S + αs, and the same for N. Older assignments fade, so centroids track recent data. The research team expa Lloyd is a corner case: full batch with α = 1. On DEEP, that corner sits 1.8% above the best loss. The team tested plain gradient descent as an alternative. At its best setting, it ended 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above EMA. The authors suspect EMA wins because centroids always stay inside the hull of their assigned points. What replaces hyperparameter tuning? Two fitted scaling laws set batch size B and initial step α0 from dataset size n, cluster count k and epochs T. On held-out datasets, median regret was 0.07% for the step law. The step then follows a cosine schedule from α0 to 0.1α0. What else changed? Dead-cluster revival: clusters below a size threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. Finalization: training ends on each cluster’s exact last-epoch mean. Fused GPU kernels: nearest-centroid assignment is fused, so saved epochs become saved seconds. [EMBED: e-means interactive explainer] How fast is e-means in benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported by the authors. Epochs: e-means beats Lloyd’s 25-epoch loss in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs. GPU: 10-45x wall-clock speedup against Flash-KMeans . CPU: 8-15x speedup against Faiss k-means. VIBE benchmark: all 11 embedding datasets needed 1.6 to 2.4 epochs. Billion scale: DINO10B, 10 billion 1,024-dim embeddings, split into 16.7M clusters in 2.5 epochs. The release thread shows a 1-CPU-thread demo. Lloyd took 4.39 s for 25 epochs. e-means took 0.43 s for 2.2 epochs. One Lloyd step touched 100,000 points (0.176 s). One e-means step touched 512 points (0.001 s). Mini-batch noise also helps escape bad local minima. On a 5-blob toy, Lloyd stayed stuck on 46% of 200 starts. e-means stayed stuck on 0%. Revival matters at large k. On DEEP with 16,384 clusters, proportional splitting left 47 dead clusters (0.3%). With revival off, 4,313 clusters (26.3%) died. How does e-means compare with other k-means options? The post MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. oldContent: MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ An Artificial Intelligence News Platform Wed, 11 Nov 2026 07:38:58 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.marktechpost.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cropped-Favicon-512-x-512-1-1-32x32.png MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ 32 32 127842392 MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/10/ifm-pan-2-open-world-model/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 07:38:57 +0000 https://www.marktechpost.com/?p=83850 The Institute of Foundation Models at MBZUAI released PAN 2, an Apache 2.0 world model that couples an LLM planner with a 29B diffusion transformer to simulate up to 20 seconds of action outcomes as video. The post MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. It also shipped GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It , a Chrome extension for the same data. The site reads on-demand and spot prices from each provider’s own pricing page. The goal is simple: answer “what GPU do I need, and where is it cheapest?” in one place. What is GPU Leaderboard? GPU Leaderboard is a pricing dashboard that ranks rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. It is built for teams running inference. The v1 application has 4 views: Inference pricing: a cost calculator for a full run, not a single hourly rate. Leaderboard : every offer ranked by $/GPU-hr, filterable by GPU, tier, region and availability. Cheapest Inference : the lowest on-demand floor for each tracked GPU. Providers : a directory with instance counts, regions, status-page incidents and price-check history. How does the GPU inference cost calculator work? You pick an accelerator, GPU count, duration and utilization. The calculator then prices that exact run at every provider. An optional model field narrows the list. The default example is 8×H100 for 72 hours at 90% utilization. That bills 576 GPU-hours. The cheapest result is $967.68 at Latitude, at $1.68 per GPU-hour. The median across 15 providers is $1,716.48. The most expensive is $3,545.28 at CoreWeave. The calculator also shows a “real” cost per used GPU-hour. Idle time is still billed, so $1.68 at 90% utilization becomes $1.87. This is the number most budget sheets miss. What does the Deploy It Chrome extension do? GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It brings the price data to where developers pick models. Per its store listing, it works in 3 places: Hugging Face model pages: detects model size and estimates VRAM at FP16, INT8 and INT4. It then shows the cheapest hourly GPUs that fit. GitHub repos: detects model references and gives a hardware estimate in place. Toolbar lookup: search any model or GPU from the browser toolbar. Key Takeaways GPU Leaderboard ranks 201 live GPU offers from 24 providers by $/GPU-hr. Its calculator prices a full run, including idle time at your utilization. Deploy It shows VRAM needs and cheapest GPUs on Hugging Face and GitHub. An 8×H100, 72-hour run spans $967.68 to $3,545.28 across multiple providers. Coverage and daily refresh are the main gaps versus older trackers. Try it at gpuleaderboard.com and install the Deploy It extension from the Chrome Web Store. The post MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Tue, 10 Nov 2026 21:08:13 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Exclusive: Nubank Alum Raises $14M For Colombia’s Palomma To Tackle Rent Payments, Landlord Financing https://news.crunchbase.com/fintech/nubank-alum-colombia-startup-palomma-ai-rental-services/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 13:00:04 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94369 In 2020, Cipriano Echavarría was working at Morgan Stanley in New York and weighing his next career move when he noticed a plaque on his desk. Among the names of people who had sat there before him was David Vélez . He looked up the name. Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank . Echavarría took a photo of the plaque and messaged him on LinkedIn , asking for career advice. It turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with plans to eventually start a company of his own. Felipe Monsalve, Cipriano Echavarría and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, founders of Palomma. (Courtesy photo) Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma , has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned. The financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital , Clocktower Technology Ventures , Tekton Ventures , Simma Capital and Yango Ventures , alongside existing investors Y Combinator , 17Sigma , Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures . Palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume. The company will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría said Colombia remains the priority. “We want to win Colombia,” he said in an interview. Finding a business in rent payments Palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners. After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo , MIT -trained engineers with experience at Meta , Cobre and JP Morgan . The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent. It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said. Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties. The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled. From software to financial services Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the company a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products. From there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and credit-building benefits, while Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront. Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults. The company is also developing Palomma Flex, which would let tenants split their monthly rent into two installments. Property managers pay a subscription fee for the AI software, and Palomma earns a percentage of rent through its payments and financial services. Getting customers to adopt more of its services has helped drive Palomma’s growth. The company reports net revenue retention of 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from an existing group of customers nearly quadrupled, even after accounting for customers who left or spent less. Overall, the decision to combine AI leasing software, payments and financial services reflects Echavarría’s view of what it takes to build a large business in Latin America. He pointed to U.S. companies such as EliseAI , Bilt , TheGuarantors and Flex as comparisons for different parts of Palomma’s business. Echavarría believes that reaching a similar scale in Latin America requires a wider range of products. “In the U.S., you can build one solution and be really large because the market allows it,” he said. “In Latin America, if you want to be really large, you need to do all the things.” Managing the risk AI also helps decide which tenants qualify for rental guarantees. Palomma’s leasing agent communicates through WhatsApp and collects application documents. The company claims that it can then deliver an approval in under 30 seconds. The company draws on information from leasing conversations and rental payment behavior to assess applicants. The company’s rental guarantees put Palomma on the hook if tenants don’t pay. The startup initially takes on that risk itself, but Echavarría told Crunchbase News it was working to finalize a partnership with an insurer that would share the risk and let Palomma offer more guarantees. The startup is also using AI to keep its team small. As of Nov. 4, it had 18 employees, up from about 14 when it closed its Series A roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer service employee works alongside AI agents to support the roughly 200,000 tenants paying rent through Palomma’s platform, Echavarría said. The startup operates on the premise that AI can make real estate financial services cheaper to provide, much as mobile technology helped digital banks compete with lenders that maintained large branch networks. Longer term, Palomma also plans to expand beyond rentals into homeowners association payments and residential property transactions. Pepe Bolaños , managing partner at Cometa, said Palomma stood out for its founding team and the opportunity to modernize Latin America’s fragmented rental market. In Colombia alone, nearly 8 million households rent their homes, he noted. “We look for companies tackling markets where outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset that can be leveraged and monetized through AI,” he wrote via email. Bolaños pointed to Echavarría’s experience helping scale Nubank, and Monsalve and del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds. In roughly 18 months, Palomma grew to process around $130 million in monthly rental payments and serve more than 200,000 tenants with about 14 employees, he said. “That kind of execution is unusual.
